# Law of refraction, image formation and vision (`refraction_optics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, trigonometry, lenses, camera_obscura
- Core idea: We see because light from the sun or a lamp bounces off things and enters the eye; the eye sends out nothing. Light travels in straight lines, reflects at equal angles, and bends when it passes between air and water or glass: the sine of the angle from the surface normal in air divided by the sine of the angle in the denser medium is a fixed number (about 1.33 for water, about 1.5 for glass). An ideal lens brings rays from one object point to one image point; the eye is such a lens with the retina as the screen, and the image on it is upside down. Cheap demonstrations: a coin at the bottom of a cup comes into view when water is poured in; a stick looks broken at the water surface.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying the bending angle is simply proportional to the incoming angle (only roughly true for small angles)
  - Repeating the ancient view that sight goes out from the eye, or accepting it out of politeness
  - Claiming an upside-down retinal image means we should see the world upside down
  - Confusing reflection with refraction
- History: greece: c. 300 BC – Euclid, Optics (visual rays leave the eye); c. 160 AD Ptolemy measures refraction in tables, without the sine law; china: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – Mohist Canon on shadows, pinhole images and mirrors; no law of refraction; islamic: c. 984 – Ibn Sahl states a rule equivalent to the sine law; c. 1011–1021 Ibn al-Haytham shows that vision is light entering the eye; europe: 1602 – Harriot finds the sine law (unpublished); 1604 Kepler explains the retinal image; 1621 Snell; 1637 Descartes publishes the law
- Read:
  - Ibn al-Haytham, Kitab al-Manazir (c. 1011–1021; tr. A. I. Sabra, The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham, 1989)
  - David C. Lindberg, Theories of Vision from al-Kindi to Kepler (1976)
  - A. Mark Smith, From Sight to Light: The Passage from Ancient to Modern Optics (2015)
